summary: Living ponderosa pine lookout tree on Kaibab NF near Fredonia, AZ, NRHP-listed 1992; build date, staffing and current condition not confirmed.

facts.design: Living three-trunked ponderosa pine with a spiked ladder up its east side
facts.status_note: The 1990 nomination form says the tree is still alive with its ladder intact; no source we read confirms its condition today

access.note: On Kaibab National Forest land off Forest Road 248; no source we read describes access to this tree specifically

facts.agency: USDA Forest Service, Kaibab National Forest

events.note: Forest Service nomination form, prepared May 1990, describes the tree as still alive with its ladder intact
Listed on the National Register on January 13, 1992 (NRIS 91001962) as one of eleven Kaibab lookout trees

evidence.supports: Lookout trees are the survivors of a system that used tall, straight trees as vantage points
evidence.quote: the survivors of a system of improvised fire lookout towers that used tall, straight trees as vantage points

evidence.supports: Many of these lookouts were established between 1905 and 1920
evidence.quote: Many of these lookouts were established between 1905 and 1920.

evidence.supports: All eleven trees were listed on the National Register on January 13, 1992
evidence.quote: All were individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places on January 13, 1992.

evidence.supports: Cooper Ridge Lookout Tree is one of the listed trees, reference 91001962
evidence.quote: Cooper Ridge Lookout Tree , reference number 91001962

evidence.supports: Coordinates of the Cooper Ridge Lookout Tree
Forest Service workers went to the highest vista, found the tallest tree, and built a ladder and platform on it
evidence.quote: Forest Service employees would hike up to the highest vista in an area and from there would find the tallest tree. They would then construct a ladder against the side of the tree and saw off the top, building a platform on the flattened trunk.

evidence.supports: Only 11 of the trees were located
evidence.quote: only 11 were located

evidence.supports: Each platform was staffed by two people, a lookout and a patrolman
evidence.quote: Each was staffed by two people: a lookout who kept an eye on the horizon for wisps of smoke, and a patrolman who would run towards early fires

evidence.supports: Steel towers eventually replaced the trees
evidence.quote: as more steel towers were constructed the trees were eventually phased out and forgotten

evidence.supports: Atlas Obscura's map coordinates lead to the Tusayan tree, which it calls likely the most accessible
evidence.quote: The map coordinates lead to the Tusayan Lookout Tree, which is likely the most accessible due to its proximity to a paved road.

evidence.supports: Most trees require seasonally passable dirt roads and sometimes hiking
evidence.quote: to reach most of the trees you'll have to drive down dirt roads that are only seasonably passable, depending on the weather and your vehicle, and even from there some hiking may be required

evidence.supports: Tree is located west of FR 248, 0.7 miles north of Highway 67
evidence.quote: located west of FR 248 just .7 miles north of Highway 67

evidence.supports: Tree is on the North Kaibab Ranger District of Kaibab National Forest
evidence.quote: on the North Kaibab Ranger District, Kaibab National Forest

evidence.supports: Ridge location northeast of Moquitch Canyon
evidence.quote: an unnamed ridge northeast of Moquitch Canyon

evidence.supports: Tree is a three-trunked ponderosa pine about 75 feet tall, with a ladder up its east side
evidence.quote: This lookout tree is a squatty (three trunks) ponderosa pine measuring 75 feet high and 4 feet in diameter with a ladder constructed up its eastern side

evidence.supports: Five sections of ladder remain
evidence.quote: Five contiguous segments of ladder works remain.

evidence.supports: Ladder is attached to the tree with spikes
evidence.quote: attached to the tree with spikes

evidence.supports: Construction and abandonment dates are unknown; oral history might establish them
evidence.quote: The construction and abandonment dates for the Cooper Ridge Lookout Tree are presently unknown. They might be ascertained, however, through oral history.

evidence.supports: Tree had been abandoned for approximately 30 years by the 1990 form
evidence.quote: abandoned for approximately 30 years

evidence.supports: Form says North Kaibab lookout trees fell out of use in the late 1960s
evidence.quote: lookout trees on the North Kaibab Ranger District fell out of use

evidence.supports: Tree is still alive and its ladder is in good condition
evidence.quote: The tree is still alive.

evidence.supports: Ladder is in good condition
evidence.quote: The ladder is in good condition.

evidence.supports: Nomination prepared in May 1990
evidence.quote: May 1990

evidence.supports: Listing date of 1/13/92
Tree is in Coconino County
evidence.quote: county Coconino

corrections.why: Sources describe a living pine with a ladder and platform, not a tower
The NRHP form gives the county as Coconino

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1990 form says the tree had been abandoned for approximately 30 years, which points to about 1960, but the same form says North Kaibab lookout trees fell out of use in the late 1960s; the story reports both and does not reconcile them
Atlas Obscura's map coordinates lead to the Tusayan tree, not Cooper Ridge; this record and Wikipedia place the point at Cooper Ridge

sources.title: Lookout trees in Kaibab National Forest
Cooper Ridge Lookout Tree, National Register of Historic Places Registration Form (NRIS 91001962)

notes_for_editor: The record is the Wikipedia group page but its point is the Cooper Ridge tree, so the story is about Cooper Ridge with group context from the other ten NRHP-listed trees. Build date, staffing and current condition are not in any source read. Leads: the 1987 Multiple Property Submission (Steere) for the group, Kaibab NF North Kaibab Ranger District for current condition, and the NRHP form's suggestion that oral history could date construction. Ask whether the other ten trees need their own records. The NRHP PDF's OCR text reads the fell-out-of-use date as "late 1960*8", so check the scan before relying on the late 1960s date.
